name: RLB
headline: An engineering team. On your machine.
summary: A local-first AI engineering runtime. Specialized agents plan, implement, test, and review software under human supervision.
problem: AI development tools often move the workspace and execution into hosted infrastructure. RLB explores an engineering organization that operates where the developer’s code already lives.
users: Developers who want supervised agent workflows with local execution and remote visibility.
architecture: Durable worker → specialized agents → staging → approval
Local project + Git + SQLite durable state
Outbound connection → cloud control plane → web console
features: Authenticated device pairing and remote commands
Event catch-up and private review artifacts
Staging, promotion, testing, and review workflows
challenge: Separate remote control from execution ownership. Preserve approvals, workflow state, and recovery on the local machine while exposing selected events to the cloud.
limitations: The Windows-first implementation is undergoing an architecture transition. Windows installer acceptance and live hosted account/deployment acceptance still require external environments. Local deterministic checks do not certify those deployments.
lesson: Local-first architecture is an ownership decision: remote visibility does not require relocating the codebase.

name: NYRC
headline: A little presence. A serious assistant.
summary: A desktop companion with persistent identity, memory, reminders, and optional intelligence. The provider can change. The companion stays.
problem: A useful personal companion should retain its identity and everyday tools independently of a cloud account or a particular AI provider.
users: People who want a persistent desktop presence and practical local tools; developers exploring a shared interface for future companion devices.
architecture: Semantic Body API → desktop / virtual bodies
features: Session timers and durable reminders with restart recovery
Pocket storage, saved aliases, routines, and personality settings
Desktop and virtual bodies; authenticated loopback transport
challenge: Keep intelligence separate from authority. Typed actions and host confirmations bound what an AI suggestion or connected body can do.
limitations: Unsigned release candidate. Native core acceptance is documented for macOS Apple silicon; other platforms require external desktop acceptance. Physical hardware adapters and voice recognition/synthesis are planned, not shipped.
lesson: Separating identity, intelligence, permissions, and presentation allows the companion to remain useful with AI switched off.

name: SIRL
headline: Evidence first. Explanation second.
summary: Survey validation that combines rules, statistics, and anomaly detection into inspectable risk. AI explains the evidence; it does not rewrite the score.
problem: Field survey data can contain impossible values, missing identifiers, statistical drift, and unusual response patterns. Supervisors need defensible evidence to prioritize investigation.
users: Survey supervisors and administrators investigating data quality in a hackathon/demo workflow.
architecture: CSV / eSIGMA JSON → canonical schema → Parquet
SIRL profiling → rules + statistics + Isolation Forest
features: Record evidence drill-down and hierarchical analytics
Investigation workflow, audit trail, CSV and Excel export
challenge: Avoid treating unusual records as invalid. Hard-rule violations and statistical/ML review flags have distinct classifications; deterministic fallbacks keep the workflow usable without AI.
limitations: Synthetic/demo extracts, hackathon-scale SQLite and Parquet, and no production eSIGMA authentication/VPN acceptance. Core validation APIs are intentionally unauthenticated in this build; demo login is not production RBAC.
lesson: Explainability is part of the architecture: an explanation layer should not acquire authority over the underlying evidence.

name: StockSense
headline: Every movement has a history.
summary: A database-backed workspace for products, locations, receipts, deliveries, transfers, and stock adjustments — connected by an auditable movement ledger.
problem: Inventory operations need a consistent record of what moved, where it moved, and why. Products, locations, and operational changes must remain connected.
users: Inventory managers and warehouse staff managing the stock lifecycle across locations.
features: Receipts, deliveries, internal transfers, and adjustments
Movement history, low-stock indicators, and OTP authentication
challenge: Enforce business invariants on the server: reject invalid location hierarchies, check stock availability on delivery, and preserve total stock during internal transfers.
limitations: Repository documentation describes the implementation. A public deployment, customer usage, and production acceptance have not been independently verified.
lesson: Business software earns clarity through explicit data relationships and server-side rules, with the ledger preserving an inspectable history.
